newsitem.title: USA: U.S. business community upbeat on Hong Kong.
newsitem.headline: U.S. business community upbeat on Hong Kong.

text.p: As Hong Kong officially assumed the new status as a Special Administration Region of China, many U.S. business professionals see greater opportunity in Hong Kong in the new era.

At a sumptuous reception with satellite link broadcast, many Americans joined ethnic Chinese guests in cheers as the Buahinia Hong Kong flag and the five-star Chinese flag rose at middnight Hong Kong time.
Richard Tomasetti, who heads an engineering consulting firm, Thornton-Tomsetti, welcomed the change with enthusiasm.
"I think it will be beneficial for many businesses in the United States," he said.
Tomasetti said that in the past, British firms often enjoyed preferential treatment in Hong Kong when they bid for lucrative contracts, but now American firms could compete with fewer impediments.
"I really think it will be a fairer game for us in the building industry," he said.
But some business professionals were wary of the direction of change in Hong Kong.
"I give it a 50-50 chance (for success)," said a Hong Kong native who is working for a U.S. money center bank. He said he feared that while corruption may not spread overnight, red tape may increase.
The banker noted that fears about the potential that business costs might rise in Hong Kong had already prompted some multinational companies to relocate regional headquarters to Singapore.
Hong Kong's new government would make its imprint on the life of the people, said Peter Tichansky, president of the Business Council for International Understanding.
"I don't think things will stay the same," he said. "You get new ideas and new people. Eventually things will change.
American businesses must adapt to the changes in Hong Kong, he said, adding that there are many ways the government could help them.
The surge of ethnic pride as Hong Kong returned to Chinese rule as shown on the giant screen through satellite link was considered justfied by the momentous occasion.
"It is truly a historical moment," said Estelle Cashman from the office of the president of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Cashman said she was very impressed by the caliber of the new team led by the chief executive Tung Chee Hwa. She had met Anson Chan, the Administrative Secretary, who visited the university earlier this year.
"With people like Anson Chan in the leadership, I am hopeful for Hong Kong's future," she said.
The reception marking the estblishment of Hong Kong Special Administrative Region was hosted by the Hong Kong Economic and Trade Office in New York.
Ambassador Qui Shenyung, Consul General of the People's Republic of China and Jeffrey Ling, Consul General of Great Britain, were honored guests at the event.
